turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Hey, I grabbed your vitals while you were waiting. Blood pressure was one thirty-two over eighty-four, pulse a hundred and eight, oxygen sat ninety-eight percent, and respirations sixteen.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, yeah, that pulse sounds about like what it's been doing, that jumpy thing.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, one second, this screen just froze again. Alright. What brought you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, so my heart's been racing, these palpitations, and I get short of breath with it. It's worse at night, when I'm just lying there trying to sleep.

[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The palpitations and the breathlessness have been about three weeks. It's really bad before his exams and those work meetings. He gets wiped out, and he won't tell you that part.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three weeks is a stretch. The palpitations have been more like a week, maybe a week-ish, mostly at night. And I'm not wiped out, I just notice my heart. She worries, that's why my wife came.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the chart jumped. Can you say the night part again? I only half heard it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, at night, lying in bed, my heart takes off and I can't catch my breath. Daytime it's quieter unless I've got an exam or a meeting coming up.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with that?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no chest pain. It's not pain.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Getting over here was a nightmare though. I-94 was just dead stopped, and then it started pouring.
[SEG0012] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We sat there forty minutes. The sky went that weird green-gray, like before a tornado movie.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): And the guy in the truck next to us was blasting a podcast about grilling, full volume, windows down, in the rain. I couldn't believe it.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Yeah, that storm came out of nowhere. My lunch got soaked walking over from the garage.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Did you see the lightning over the river? Looked fake, honestly. And then the parking garage was full, we circled forever.
[SEG0016] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Third level, finally. Somebody had parked a huge pickup across two spots.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Classic. Okay, sorry, I drifted. Um. Coffee. Do you drink much coffee?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh yeah, a lot. Between grad school and work I kind of live on it. Like four or five cups, and then energy drinks on top, Celsius, or Monster if the store's out.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, someone pinged me on here. How many energy drinks did you say?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Two a day. Well, actually, three if I've got an exam. Yeah, three on those days.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he vapes. Constantly. In the car, in the apartment, those little mango ones.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not constantly. I vape, yeah, nicotine, a few times a day. Not cigarettes or anything.
[SEG0023] person_1 (NURSE): Any allergies to medicines, food, anything? I need it in the chart before labs.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing I know of. No allergies.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): You taking any medicines? Prescription or over the counter?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. My roommate takes propranolol for his heart and I tried one of his once, ten milligrams, but that was his pill, I don't take it.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, wait, I had an albuterol inhaler way back for asthma when I was a kid. I stopped. Haven't used it since I was like sixteen.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any fainting, or feeling like you'll pass out?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I haven't fainted. I stay conscious, it just feels weird.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever? Chills?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I feel fine otherwise. I think this is getting built up bigger than it is.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets panicky, though, before those meetings. Sweaty, pacing the kitchen. He won't say it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not panicky. I'm not stressed, I just have a lot on. I do get a little sweaty, but that's the heart thing, not anxiety.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): You said no pain. When the heart races, is there any pressure or tightness at all?

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah. When it really kicks off there's this tight band across my chest. I wouldn't call it pain, but it's tight, and it eases off when the racing settles. Sorry, I said no before.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): It piles up mostly at night, and, um, in the ten minutes before I have to talk in class or at work.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen a second. Deep breath. Lungs are clear. Heart rhythm is regular, just fast, and I don't hear a murmur.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're comfortable sitting, and I don't see any swelling in the ankles.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it bad, though? My cousin had some heart thing, but that's a whole other story, he lives in Phoenix and he just texts me memes. Not really relevant.

[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): You said about a week, your wife said three weeks, so I'll leave it as roughly one to three weeks, not pinned down. My take, and this is provisional, is the coffee, the energy drinks, and the vaping are stirring up these palpitations, especially before exams.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): I also can't rule out a rhythm problem or a thyroid issue. Either one could look like this, so I'm not calling it yet.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Thyroid? Nobody in my family has that. My mom takes something for her cholesterol, not her thyroid.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): I want an ECG today, and blood for thyroid, a TSH. Both of those, before you leave, if the lab can fit you.
[SEG0044] person_1 (NURSE): I can walk you to ECG after we finish, and the lab's open till four.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): When it hits at night, try slow breathing. In for four counts, out for six. Do that as it starts. It's a tool, not a cure.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): In for four, out for six. Okay, I can try that. I still don't think this is a stress thing, though.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): You don't have to call it stress. Cutting the coffee and the energy drinks way down, and easing off the vape, will tell us a lot. I'd like you to start that this week.
[SEG0048] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll move the Monsters to the back of the fridge. He'll be annoyed for a day.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't hide my stuff. I'll cut back, I said I would. Probably. Mostly.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in two weeks, and we'll go over the results. Reception can book it on the way out.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, yeah. What if it gets really bad at night before that?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you faint, or that chest tightness stays and won't let up, go to the ER. Don't wait on my clinic.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Got it. Um, the ECG, that's the sticky pads, right? I had one for a sports physical in high school and the gel was freezing. Random, sorry.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yeah, sticky pads, a few minutes. Thyroid is one tube of blood. This note just vanished on me. Did you ever count how fast the pulse gets at home?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't actually know the number. It feels super fast. I almost said two hundred, but that's me being dramatic, I never counted.
[SEG0056] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I counted once and it was like a hundred and twenty, but that was right after he ran up the stairs, so maybe throw that out.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): After stairs, yeah, I'd ignore that number. We'll let the ECG talk. She'll walk you down, and I'll see you in two weeks.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Chest pain was specifically asked about and denied initially: patient said 'No, no chest pain. It's not pain.' This negative finding should be recorded alongside the later clarification of chest tightness.
Chills were specifically asked about and denied ('No fever'). The denial of chills is missing.
Patient reported no presyncope: when asked about 'feeling like you'll pass out,' he said no and that he stays conscious. This denied finding is missing.

Medication history is incomplete/wrongly represented: patient is not taking any current medicines, and specifically said he tried his roommate's propranolol once, 10 mg, but does not take it. The absence of current medications and the one-time propranolol exposure are not recorded.
Past medical history of childhood asthma is implied by the discontinued albuterol inhaler ('had an albuterol inhaler way back for asthma when I was a kid'). The asthma history itself is not recorded.
Physical exam finding missing: doctor noted the patient was comfortable sitting.
